name: Disease word next to the product
description: A disease is named nearby, in a heading, a FAQ question or navigation, while the product claim itself stays in structure/function wording. Read together, the page says the product is for that disease.

examples.text: Heading 'Living with arthritis' above 'Supports joint comfort.*'
examples.why: The heading supplies the disease the claim is about.

examples.text: FAQ: 'Can I take it for my high blood pressure?' Answer: 'Many customers do.'
examples.why: The answer endorses a disease use without stating it.

examples.text: Shop by condition: Diabetes > Blood Sugar Support Formula
examples.why: Navigation organised by disease (FDA cited this in 2025).

usual_fix: Remove the disease framing (heading, FAQ or navigation); keep the structure/function claim only if substantiated.

name: Testimonials that describe disease results
description: The company's own copy is careful, but reviews or quotes on the same page describe treating a disease or dramatic results.

examples.text: 'I have MS and this makes the day easier' shown under a careful product description
examples.why: The review supplies a disease use.

examples.text: 'My doctor took me off my blood pressure pills' in a customer quote
examples.why: Implies the product replaces a drug.

examples.text: Video testimonial: 'My eczema cleared up in a week'
examples.why: A disease outcome, presented as typical.

usual_fix: Remove disease and dramatic-result testimonials; keep ones about taste, label or routine.

name: Implied before/after
description: No 'before' or 'after' words, but the order of the text, dates or numbers set up a transformation story.

examples.text: 'Week 1: 3 coffees a day.' ... 'Week 6: one.'
examples.why: Order and numbers imply a result over time.

examples.text: 'I used to dread stairs. Now I take them two at a time.'
examples.why: A transformation without the words.

examples.text: Two photos side by side captioned 'January' and 'March'
examples.why: Before/after framing through captions.

usual_fix: Remove the transformation framing or substantiate typical results and show them clearly.

name: Headline stronger than the fine print
description: The headline or hero line promises an outcome; the body or footer quietly takes it back.

examples.text: Headline 'Sharper focus from day one'; footer 'We make no health-outcome claims.'
examples.why: The footer contradicts the headline.

examples.text: 'Double your strength*' ... '*in one study of trained athletes using a different form'
examples.why: The asterisk changes the claim, out of sight.

examples.text: Subject line 'Your joint pain fix'; email body only lists ingredients
examples.why: The subject line carries the claim.

usual_fix: Bring the headline down to what the fine print and evidence support.

name: Study doesn't match the claim
description: A real study is cited, but its population, dose, form or outcome differs from what the copy implies.

examples.text: 'Clinically studied ingredient' (study used 3x the dose in the product)
examples.why: Dose mismatch.

examples.text: 'Proven to improve memory' citing a study in people with impaired circulation
examples.why: Population mismatch.

examples.text: 'Studies show omega-3 supports the heart' for a product with a different EPA/DHA ratio
examples.why: Formulation mismatch.

usual_fix: State the population and dose the study covers, or remove the claim.

name: Natural, safe, no side effects, detox
description: Words that imply safety or purity ('natural', 'gentle', 'no side effects', 'detox', 'flush toxins') suggest a safety or health claim the company can't support.

examples.text: '100% natural, so it's safe to take with anything'
examples.why: Natural is not proof of safety; it implies no interactions.

examples.text: 'Flush the toxins your liver can't handle'
examples.why: Implies a liver problem and a detox effect.

examples.text: 'Gentle enough for the whole family'
examples.why: Implies safety for children and pregnancy.

usual_fix: Remove the safety implication; keep the relevant warnings.

name: Positioned against drugs or medical care
description: The copy sets the product up as an alternative to medicine, doctors or prescriptions without naming a disease.

examples.text: 'Why reach for pills when nature has an answer?'
examples.why: Positions the product as a drug substitute.

examples.text: 'What Big Pharma doesn't want you to know'
examples.why: Implies suppressed medical efficacy.

examples.text: 'Skip the pharmacy line'
examples.why: Implies it replaces medication.

name: Hedged claim repeated until it reads as a promise
description: Each use says 'may' or 'helps', but the same benefit appears so often that the page reads as a promise.

examples.text: 'May support joint comfort' five times across one landing page
examples.why: Repetition outweighs the hedge.

examples.text: 'Helps you build muscle' in the subject line, hero, bullets and CTA
examples.why: The core message becomes the claim.

examples.text: Every social post in a series ends with 'may boost immunity'
examples.why: Repetition across a campaign.

usual_fix: Group into one decision; keep the claim once with clear limits, or remove it.

name: Fear or urgency tied to a health outcome
description: Scarcity, deadlines or fear are linked to a health consequence of not buying.

examples.text: 'Every day without omega-3, your heart pays the price. Only 12 left.'
examples.why: Fear of a disease outcome plus scarcity.

examples.text: 'Don't wait until your joints give out'
examples.why: Implies prevention of joint disease.

examples.text: 'Cold season is here. Stock up before it's too late.'
examples.why: Implies cold prevention with urgency.

usual_fix: Remove the health fear; check any scarcity claim is true.

name: Disclaimer or 'research only' label that the copy contradicts
description: A disclaimer ('not intended to treat any disease', 'for research use only') sits beside copy that does exactly what it disclaims. FDA and FTC treat the claim as made.

examples.text: 'Reduces arthritis pain.* (*Not intended to treat any disease)'
examples.why: The disclaimer directly contradicts the claim.

examples.text: 'For laboratory use only' on a product with dosing instructions and mood reviews
examples.why: Marketing shows human use.

examples.text: 'For entertainment purposes only' under a clear treatment claim
examples.why: Disclaimers can't negate an express claim.

usual_fix: Change the claim; the disclaimer alone never fixes it.

name: Disease implied by name, link or hashtag
description: The product name, URL slug, hashtags or image alt text name a disease while the visible copy stays careful.

examples.text: Product 'GlucoBalance' with copy about 'healthy energy'
examples.why: The name implies blood-sugar treatment.

examples.text: Link text 'Learn more' pointing to /joint-pain-relief
examples.why: The URL slug names a symptom.

examples.text: Caption ending '#arthritis #naturalcure'
examples.why: Hashtags carry the disease claim.

usual_fix: Decision for the company: rename, change the slug or remove the hashtag.
